title: Making yoghurt from goats' milk
subtitle: A thinner, naturally white set yoghurt with a clean, mild flavour.
excerpt: Goats' milk yoghurt is thinner than cows' milk yoghurt because goats' milk contains less casein and no A1 beta-casein. It does not set as firm without additives, but the flavour is clean and mild with a slight tang. Here is the method for a reliable set using either a yoghurt maker or a thermos flask.
sourceNotes: Moorlands Cheesemakers, yoghurt guide. Ricki Carroll, Home Cheese Making (2002), yoghurt chapter. National Dairy Council UK, dairy fermentation guidance.

glossaryTerms.definition: A heat-loving starter culture that works between 40–45°C. Used for yoghurt, mozzarella, and Swiss-type cheeses. The main bacteria are Streptococcus thermophilus and Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus.

content.text: Yoghurt is milk thickened by lactic acid bacteria working at incubation temperature. The bacteria used in yoghurt are
, meaning they need to be kept at 40 to 45°C for 6 to 10 hours to produce enough acid to thicken the milk. Below this temperature the bacteria work too slowly; above 50°C they die.
2 tablespoons of plain live yoghurt as a starter (commercial goats' yoghurt works; cows' milk yoghurt also works if no goats' yoghurt is available)
Heat the milk to 85°C in a clean pan, stirring to prevent scorching. Hold at 85°C for 5 minutes. This pasteurises the milk and denatures whey proteins, improving the final set.
Cool the milk to 43°C. Stir frequently to cool evenly. Check the temperature with the cheese thermometer.
Stir the starter yoghurt into 100 ml of the warm milk in a separate cup until smooth, then stir this mix back into the main batch. This prevents lumps of cold yoghurt chilling the milk.
Pour into sterilised jars and place in a yoghurt maker set to 43°C. Incubate for 8 to 10 hours without disturbing the jars.
Without a yoghurt maker: pour the inoculated milk into a warmed thermos flask. Seal and leave for 8 to 10 hours. The thermos retains enough heat for most of the incubation period.
Refrigerate immediately once set. Goats' milk yoghurt will be thinner than shop yoghurt. If you want a thicker result, drain it for 2 to 4 hours through muslin to concentrate it.

attrs.title: Why goats' milk yoghurt is white

content.text: Goats efficiently convert dietary beta-carotene to vitamin A, so their milk contains very little residual beta-carotene. Cows store some beta-carotene in milk fat, which gives cows' milk dairy products a cream or yellow tint. Goats' milk yoghurt is always bright white for this reason, regardless of the quality of the milk or the culture used.
